name: Albiglutide
lead: Albiglutide (brand names Tanzeum in the United States and Eperzan in Europe) is a once-weekly injectable glucagon-like peptide-1 (GLP-1) receptor agonist that was approved to improve blood-sugar control in adults with type 2 diabetes. It was developed by Human Genome Sciences and marketed by GlaxoSmithKline (GSK) [11][1].

It is a fusion protein made of two copies of a modified human GLP-1 sequence attached to human albumin, a design that slows its breakdown and lets it be dosed weekly [11][1]. It was approved in Europe in March 2014 and in the US in April 2014, and GSK announced a worldwide withdrawal in 2017 for economic reasons [11].

Albiglutide was never approved for weight loss. It appears in a looksmaxxing-adjacent wiki because it belongs to the GLP-1 class of drugs that has become prominent in fat-loss discussions. Trials in diabetes reported modest weight effects, and a 2015 analysis cited on Wikipedia found it less effective than other GLP-1 agonists on both blood-sugar and weight measures [11].

paras: The approved use was as an add-on to diet and exercise for adults with type 2 diabetes [1][11]. It was not approved for obesity or cosmetic weight management, and no trial in the registry set out to test it as a weight-loss drug.

Like other GLP-1 receptor agonists, albiglutide mimics the gut hormone GLP-1, which raises insulin secretion when glucose is high, lowers glucagon, slows gastric emptying and may reduce appetite [4][3]. Native GLP-1 is degraded within a few minutes in the circulation, so analogues have been engineered for longer action [4].

Albiglutide is a recombinant protein of about 645 amino acids produced in yeast, in which a single amino acid change protects the GLP-1 portion from the enzyme DPP-4, and the albumin portion extends its life in the body [11]. Peak levels occur 3 to 5 days after an injection and the elimination half-life is about 5 days [11].

In the HARMONY phase 3 programme, albiglutide lowered HbA1c versus placebo and added to other diabetes drugs [1][13]. In HARMONY 7, a head-to-head open-label trial against daily liraglutide, albiglutide met non-inferiority criteria on the pre-specified margin but is reported to have produced smaller reductions in HbA1c and body weight [9][11].
Systematic reviews and mixed-treatment comparisons place it at the lower end of the class for HbA1c and weight reduction [5][10][11].

Reported common effects in trials include diarrhoea, nausea, injection-site reactions and, with other glucose-lowering drugs, hypoglycaemia [11]. Gastrointestinal events are the most frequently reported class-wide adverse events in GLP-1 trials [7]. Acute pancreatitis (about 0.3% in trials) and hypersensitivity were reported as uncommon [11].

The US label carried a boxed warning about thyroid C-cell tumours, based on rodent findings seen with the class, and listed medullary thyroid carcinoma and multiple endocrine neoplasia type 2 as contraindications [11][1].

Human Genome Sciences invented the molecule and developed it with GSK, which later acquired the company. GSK filed for US approval in January 2013 and for European approval in March 2013 [11]. The European Commission approved it in March 2014 and the US FDA in April 2014 [11].
In 2017 GSK announced it would withdraw the drug worldwide by July 2018, citing economic reasons [11][1].

Albiglutide was tested in a large phase 2 and 3 programme in type 2 diabetes, including trials in renal impairment, Japanese patients and comparisons with liraglutide [13]. The Harmony Outcomes trial randomised patients with type 2 diabetes and cardiovascular disease to albiglutide or placebo to assess major cardiovascular events [12]. A meta-analysis of GLP-1 agonist cardiovascular outcome trials also included it [2]. A paediatric trial and an insulin add-on trial were registered but withdrawn before enrolment [13]. No trial studied it as an appearance or body-composition treatment in people without diabetes.

card.summary: A withdrawn once-weekly GLP-1 diabetes drug; it was never a weight-loss product and produced modest weight effects in trials.
card.note: No longer marketed anywhere; approved only for type 2 diabetes.

quick.overview:
Albiglutide was a weekly injection for type 2 diabetes in the same drug class as semaglutide and liraglutide. It was approved in 2014 and pulled from the market by GSK in 2017-2018 for commercial reasons.

It was never licensed for weight loss, and published comparisons rate its weight and blood-sugar effects as smaller than those of other drugs in its class.
quick.mechanism: It is a modified GLP-1 fused to albumin, which resists breakdown and lasts about five days in the body. It activates GLP-1 receptors, which raises insulin release after meals, lowers glucagon and slows stomach emptying.
quick.risks: Reported effects include nausea, diarrhoea and injection-site reactions, with pancreatitis uncommon. The label carried a boxed warning about thyroid C-cell tumours seen in rodent studies of the class. It is no longer sold.
